syntax: console.log(42, "hi", true, null, [1, 2], { a: 1 });
explain: Values: numbers, strings, booleans, null/undefined, arrays [ ] and objects { }. Everything JavaScript works with is a value.
example: po.wor: the planner stores lines as an array of strings.
remember: Six things: number, string, boolean, nothing, list [ ], object { }.

explain: Variables are names for values. const can't be reassigned; let can.
example: po.wor: const lines = …
remember: const = constant (stays), let = let it change.

explain: Expressions: anything that makes a value. Operators (+ * > && ===) combine values into new values.
example: po.wor: if (text.startsWith("#") && …)
remember: If you can console.log it, it is an expression.

explain: A function is reusable code. You call it with ( ) and give it arguments; return sends a value back. An arrow => is a shorter function. Functions are values too.
example: po.wor: function render() { … }
remember: Name it, ( ) to call it, return to answer.

syntax:
const user = { name: "Po", greet() { return "hi " + this.name; } };
console.log(user.name, user["name"], user.greet());
explain: Objects hold named values (properties). Read them with a dot. A function stored in an object is called a method.
example: po.wor: localStorage.getItem(…), document.body
remember: Dot = "open the object and take…".

explain: Control flow: if / else choose, for / while repeat. Blocks { } group statements.
example: po.wor: looping over planner lines.
remember: if = choose, for = repeat, { } = the group.

syntax:
document.body.addEventListener("click", () => console.log("clicked"));
document.body.click();
explain: An event listener is just a method call with a function as an argument. The browser calls your function later, when the event happens.
example: po.wor: every button on the site.
remember: object.method("what", whatToDo)

syntax: console.log([1, 2, 3].map((n) => n * 2).filter((n) => n > 2).join(", "));
explain: Chaining: each method returns a value, so you put another dot on it. map, filter and join are methods on arrays, given functions.
example: po.wor: lines.map(…).join("\n")
remember: Read it left to right: each dot works on the last answer.

syntax:
const time = "14:05";
console.log(`meeting ${time}`);
explain: A template literal is a string with expressions inside ${ }.
example: po.wor: the /t time stamp.
remember: Backticks + ${ } = "fill in the blank".

explain: The DOM is the page as objects. Changing the page = calling methods and setting properties on those objects.
example: po.wor: building the planner rows.
remember: The page is objects; dots change it.

explain: const cannot be given a new value; let can.
example: Storing a username and a click counter.
remember: const = can't point to something new; let = can change. Start with const.

syntax:
const add = (a, b) => a + b;
console.log(add(2, 3));
explain: An arrow function: a short way to write a function that returns a + b.
example: Small helpers like formatting a price.

syntax:
const name = "Ada";
console.log(`Hello, ${name}!`);
explain: Backticks make a template string. A dollar sign and curly brackets put a value inside.
example: Building messages like "Welcome back, Ada".

explain: map changes every item into a new list. filter keeps only items that pass a test.
example: Showing only products that are in stock.

explain: An object groups values under names (keys). Read and change them with a dot.
example: Keeping all the details about one user together.

explain: if runs a block only when the check is true; else runs otherwise.
example: Showing a different page to logged-in users.

explain: for...of goes through a list one item at a time.
example: Drawing every task in a to-do list.

explain: querySelector finds an element using a CSS selector. textContent changes its text.
example: Updating a score on a game page.

explain: addEventListener runs a function every time something happens, like a click.
example: Opening a menu when you click its button.
remember: addEventListener(what happens, what to do).

explain: fetch gets data from a website. await waits for the answer without freezing the page.
example: Loading weather or posts from an API.

explain: let can change later, const cannot. Use const unless you need to change it.
example: A counter vs. a fixed setting.

syntax:
const name = "Ada";
console.log(`Hello, ${name}! You have ${2 + 3} messages.`);
explain: Backticks make a template string. ${...} puts a value inside.
example: Building messages.

syntax: console.log(typeof 42, typeof "hi", typeof true, typeof [], typeof null);
explain: typeof tells you what kind of value something is.
example: Checking input before using it.

syntax:
console.log(1 == "1");
console.log(1 === "1");
explain: == converts types first, === does not. Always use ===.
example: Avoiding surprise bugs.
remember: === checks the value and the type. Always use three.

explain: condition ? ifTrue : ifFalse is a short if/else.
example: Picking a word to show.

explain: switch compares one value to many cases. break stops it falling into the next case.
example: Menus with many options.

explain: Start; keep going while true; step. Prints 0, 1, 2.
example: Repeating something a set number of times.

explain: while repeats as long as the condition is true.
example: Retrying until something works.

explain: continue skips to the next round, break stops the loop.
example: Skipping bad data.

syntax:
const nums = [1, 2, 3];
console.log(nums.map((n) => n * 2));
explain: map makes a new array by changing every item.
example: Turning prices into prices with tax.
remember: map = change every item, same count back.

syntax:
const nums = [1, 2, 3, 4];
console.log(nums.filter((n) => n % 2 === 0));
explain: filter keeps only the items where the function returns true.
example: Showing only unfinished tasks.
remember: filter = keep the items that pass the test.

syntax:
const nums = [1, 2, 3, 4];
console.log(nums.reduce((total, n) => total + n, 0));
explain: reduce boils an array down to one value. 0 is the starting total.
example: The total of a shopping cart.
remember: reduce = squash the list into one value (start value at the end).

explain: find returns the first match. includes says if a value is in the array.
example: Looking up a user by id.

explain: push adds to the end, pop removes from the end. length is how many.
example: A stack of undo steps.

explain: slice copies a part (start, end). splice removes items from the array itself.
example: Pages of results; deleting one item.
remember: slice copies from start up to (not including) end; the list stays the same.

explain: sort with (a, b) => a - b sorts numbers small to big. Without it, numbers sort like words.
example: Sorting scores.

syntax:
["a", "b"].forEach((item, i) => console.log(i, item));
console.log("a,b,c".split(","), ["a", "b"].join(" + "));
explain: forEach runs a function for each item. split turns text into an array, join does the opposite.
example: Reading CSV text.

explain: ... spreads the items of an array or object into a new one.
example: Copying and adding without changing the original.

explain: Pull values out of arrays and objects into variables in one line.
example: Reading fields from API data.

explain: name = "friend" is a default, used when nothing is passed.
example: Optional settings.

explain: ...nums collects all the arguments into an array.
example: Functions that take any number of values.

explain: A closure: the inner function remembers the variables around it.
example: Private state, like a counter.

explain: Object.keys lists the names, Object.entries gives [name, value] pairs.
example: Showing every field of a record.

explain: ?. stops instead of crashing when something is missing. ?? gives a fallback for null/undefined.
example: Reading API data that may be missing fields.

explain: try runs code, catch handles errors, finally always runs.
example: Handling a bad file or network error.

explain: throw stops the function and sends an error to whoever called it.
example: Rejecting bad input.

explain: extends makes a class based on another. It can replace methods.
example: Different kinds of users or shapes.

syntax:
const wait = (ms) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));
wait(500).then(() => console.log("half a second later"));
explain: A Promise is a value that arrives later. then runs when it does.
example: Waiting before showing a message.

explain: setTimeout runs once after a delay; setInterval repeats until cleared.
example: Clocks, auto-save.

explain: stringify turns data into text, parse turns text back into data.
example: Saving data and sending it to a server.

syntax:
console.log(Math.round(2.5), Math.floor(2.9), Math.max(1, 5, 3));
console.log(Math.floor(Math.random() * 6) + 1);
explain: Math has rounding, max/min, and random (0 up to 1). The last line is a dice roll.
example: Games and rounding prices.

syntax: console.log(Number("42") + 1, parseInt("10px"), (3.14159).toFixed(2));
explain: Turn text into numbers. toFixed(2) keeps 2 decimals.
example: Reading numbers typed into a form.

explain: trim removes outside spaces; toUpperCase, replace and includes do what they say.
example: Cleaning up user input.

syntax:
const now = new Date();
console.log(now.getFullYear(), now.toISOString());
explain: Date holds a moment in time.
example: Showing today's date.
remember: new Date() = right now. Months count from 0.

explain: A Set keeps only unique values. A Map stores key → value pairs.
example: Removing duplicates.

syntax:
const title = document.querySelector("h1");
const items = document.querySelectorAll(".item");
explain: querySelector finds the first match, querySelectorAll finds all of them (CSS selectors).
example: Grabbing elements to change them.
remember: querySelector = the first one. querySelectorAll = all of them.

explain: classList adds or removes classes. textContent sets the text safely.
example: Opening a menu, dark mode switches.
remember: classList: add, remove, toggle, contains.

explain: Create an element, fill it, then put it on the page.
example: Adding items to a to-do list.

syntax:
localStorage.setItem("theme", "dark");
console.log(localStorage.getItem("theme"));
explain: localStorage keeps small text values in the browser, even after closing it.
example: Remembering a setting.
remember: set = save, get = read. Only text: use JSON.stringify for lists and objects.

explain: export shares code from a file, import uses it. Needs <script type="module">.
example: Splitting a big app into files.

syntax:
const time = new Date(2026, 10, 27, 14, 5).toTimeString().slice(0, 5);
console.log(time);   // 14:05
explain: toTimeString gives "14:05:00 GMT+…". slice(0, 5) keeps the first 5 characters: hours and minutes.
example: po.wor planner: type /t and a space and it turns into the time.
remember: Months count from 0, so 10 is November. slice(0, 5) = "the first five".

explain: Builds a date like 2026-11-07. getMonth is 0 to 11, so add 1. padStart adds a 0 in front of single digits.
example: po.wor planner: each day is saved as "planner:2026-11-27".
remember: getMonth() + 1 because January is 0. padStart(2, "0") = "2 wide, fill the start with 0".

explain: setDate moves the date and rolls over into the next month for you. new Date(date) makes a copy, so the original stays the same.
example: po.wor planner: the < and > buttons go back or forward a day or a week.
remember: Copy first, then change.

syntax:
const d = new Date(2026, 10, 27);
console.log(d.toLocaleDateString("en-GB", { weekday: "long", day: "numeric", month: "long" }));
explain: Writes a date in words. The first part is the language ("en-GB"), the options pick which parts to show.
example: po.wor planner: the title, like "friday 27 november 2026".
remember: Locale + options: say the language, then list the parts you want.

explain: getDay gives 0 for Sunday, 1 for Monday … 6 for Saturday. (getDay() + 6) % 7 is how many days ago Monday was.
example: po.wor planner: the week view always starts on Monday.
remember: getDay: Sunday is 0. Add 6, then % 7, and Monday becomes 0.

syntax:
const line = "• buy milk";
console.log(line.slice(2));      // buy milk
console.log(line.slice(0, 1));   // •
console.log(line.slice(-4));     // milk
explain: slice(start, end) copies part of the text. The end is not included. A minus number counts from the end.
example: po.wor planner: line.slice(2) is the text after the bullet.
remember: Cut a slice: from start up to (not including) end.

syntax:
const text = "one
two
three";
console.log(text.startsWith("one"), text.endsWith("three"));
console.log(text.indexOf("
"), text.lastIndexOf("
"));   // 3 7
explain: startsWith and endsWith answer true or false. indexOf finds the first place, lastIndexOf the last place; -1 means not found.
example: po.wor planner: lastIndexOf("\n") finds where the line you are on starts.
remember: indexOf looks from the left, lastIndexOf from the right. -1 = not there.

syntax:
console.log("5".padStart(2, "0"));        // 05
console.log("task".padEnd(8) + "ctrl+1");
explain: padStart and padEnd add characters (spaces if you don't say) until the text is that long. Good for lining things up.
example: po.wor planner: the control legend lines up its columns with padEnd.
remember: pad = fill. Start = in front, End = behind.

syntax: console.log("done".replace(/[^\u0336]/g, "$&\u0336"));   // d̶o̶n̶e̶
explain: In the replacement, $& means "the text that matched". \u0336 is a strike mark that crosses out the letter before it.
example: po.wor planner: click a ○ twice and the event is crossed out.
remember: $& = "the thing you found".

syntax:
const text = "日本語😀";
console.log(text.length, [...text].length);   // 5 4
explain: .length counts code units, and an emoji uses 2. Spreading with [...] splits it into real characters.
example: po.wor Japanese page: counting 文字数 (how many characters).
remember: Spread it out, then count.

syntax:
const m = "## Shopping".match(/^(#{1,6}) (.*)/);
console.log(m[1].length, m[2]);   // 2 Shopping
explain: match gives null (no match) or a list: m[0] is the whole match, m[1] and m[2] are the parts in ( ). ^ is the start, #{1,6} is 1 to 6 #, .* is anything.
example: po.wor planner: # to ###### make headings.
remember: ( ) = capture: what's inside each pair of brackets comes back as m[1], m[2]…

syntax:
console.log(/^[•×○] /.test("• task"));   // true
console.log("a-b-c".replace(/-/g, " "));   // a b c
console.log(/<hr>/i.test("<HR>"));         // true
explain: test answers true or false. [ ] means any one of these characters. The g flag changes every match, i ignores upper/lower case.
example: po.wor planner: checks for bullets and for <hr>.
remember: test = a yes/no question. g = global (all of them). i = insensitive (to case).

syntax: console.log("a **bold** word".split(/(\*\*[^*]+\*\*)/));
explain: When the pattern has ( ), split keeps the matched pieces in the list too: ["a ", "**bold**", " word"].
example: po.wor planner: finds **bold**, *italic*, ~~crossed~~ and `code` in a line.
remember: split with brackets = cut, but keep the piece you cut out.

explain: (?:^|\s) means "the start or a space", without capturing it. \/ is a real /, (\w+) captures the letters, and " $" means a space at the very end.
example: po.wor planner: spots /t and a space, right before the cursor.
remember: (?: ) = brackets that group but don't capture. \w = word letters.

explain: An object can hold functions. SLASH[word] looks one up by name and () runs it. It replaces a long if / else if chain.
example: po.wor planner: the /t slash word and the v d w t keys.
remember: Look it up, then call it: SLASH[word] finds it, () runs it.

explain: Object.assign copies settings onto something. Here it makes and sets up an element in one line.
example: po.wor planner: the clickable bullet span and the placeholder line.
remember: assign = "copy these settings onto it".

explain: getElementById finds the element with that id (no # needed). $ is just a short name for it that you make yourself.
example: po.wor: planner.js and japanese.js both start with this $ helper.
remember: $ is not magic: it's a function name you chose.

explain: Every element has a hidden property: true hides it, false shows it. The same as the hidden attribute in HTML.
example: po.wor planner: switching between the day and the week view.
remember: hidden = true hides, false shows.

explain: data-view="week" in HTML is button.dataset.view in JavaScript. data-some-name becomes dataset.someName.
example: po.wor planner: the day and week buttons; the 100, 200 numbers on the Japanese paper.
remember: data- disappears and the rest becomes the key. Dashes turn into camelCase.

explain: setAttribute writes any attribute, getAttribute reads it. Values are always text.
example: po.wor: the planner buttons and the Japanese tabs (aria-pressed, aria-selected).
remember: set = write, get = read. What comes back is always text.

explain: toggle with a second value: true adds the class, false removes it. No if needed.
example: po.wor planner: today's date is bold; view mode adds "reading".
remember: toggle(name, yes/no) = "have it only if yes".

explain: append adds at the end, prepend at the start; both take elements or text, several at once. after puts it right behind, replaceWith swaps it, remove deletes it.
example: po.wor: the planner rows and the Japanese sample cards.
remember: append = last, prepend = first, after = behind, replaceWith = swap, remove = gone.

explain: children is a list of elements but not a real array. [...] turns it into one, so forEach, map and filter work.
example: po.wor planner: highlighting the picked row in the suggestion list.
remember: [...] = pour it into a real array.

explain: cloneNode makes a copy of an element. true also copies everything inside it.
example: po.wor: clicking the box copies the logo into a small P that gets tossed in.
remember: clone = an identical twin.

syntax:
console.log(location.href);   // the page's address
// location.href = "box.html";   // this line would open another page
explain: location.href is the address of the page. Setting it opens that page, like clicking a link.
example: po.wor: after the box animation, location.href opens box.html.
remember: href = where this page lives. Change it and you move.

explain: The input event runs on every change while you type (change only runs when you leave the box). Changing .value in code fires nothing, so dispatchEvent fires it yourself.
example: po.wor planner: every keystroke is saved; adding a bullet with ctrl+1 dispatches "input" to save it.
remember: input = every key. change = when you're done.

explain: event.key names the key: "a", "Enter", "Escape", "ArrowLeft". ctrlKey, metaKey (⌘), altKey and shiftKey are true while held. preventDefault stops the browser's own action.
example: po.wor planner: ctrl+1 to 5 for bullets; v d w t and the arrows when you are not typing.
remember: metaKey = ⌘. preventDefault = "browser, don't do your usual thing".

explain: keydown runs when a key goes down, keyup when it comes back up. Together: do something only while a key is held.
example: po.wor planner: hold control to see the legend.
remember: down = pressed, up = let go.

explain: focus runs when you click or tab into a box, blur when you leave it. In code, input.focus() and input.blur() do the same.
example: po.wor planner: leaving a line shows its result; the phone bullet bar shows while you type.
remember: focus = you're in. blur = you left (and it goes blurry).

explain: event.target is what was clicked. matches(selector) asks "are you this?", closest(selector) looks at it and then up through its parents.
example: po.wor planner: Enter on a button presses it instead of starting to write.
remember: matches = "are you…?" closest = "are you, or any parent…?"

explain: onclick holds one function; setting it again replaces the old one. addEventListener can add many.
example: po.wor planner: each page redraw sets doc.onclick again without piling up handlers.
remember: onclick = one slot. addEventListener = as many as you like.

explain: pageshow runs every time the page appears, even when the browser brings it back from the Back button.
example: po.wor: going Back resets the box lid and removes the tossed P.
remember: show = every time you see it, not just the first load.

explain: selectionStart and selectionEnd are where the selection starts and ends (counted in characters). The same number means a plain cursor. setSelectionRange moves it.
example: po.wor planner: /t reads the text before the cursor; the cursor is put back after a bullet.
remember: start = where it begins, end = where it stops. Same number = just a cursor.

explain: A box that grows as you type. scrollHeight is the height of everything inside it. Set height to auto first so it can shrink too.
example: po.wor planner: the typing line grows instead of scrolling.
remember: auto first (shrink), then scrollHeight (grow to fit).

explain: getSelection() is the text you highlighted. String() turns it into plain text; an empty string means nothing is selected.
example: po.wor planner: if you selected text to copy, a click doesn't start typing.
remember: getSelection = what's highlighted right now.

explain: localStorage can fail (private windows, sealed-off frames). try runs it, catch keeps the page working if it fails. Here in the playground storage is blocked, so you see an empty line: that's the catch doing its job.
example: po.wor: the planner and the Japanese page save this way.
remember: Try the risky thing; catch the error so nothing breaks.

explain: a || b gives b when a is empty, null or 0. Here: use an empty list when nothing was saved.
example: po.wor Japanese page: the question queue.
remember: || = "or else use this".

explain: some asks "is at least one true?", every asks "are all of them true?". Both give true or false.
example: po.wor planner: does this line already start with a bullet?
remember: some = at least one. every = all of them.

explain: splice(where, how many to remove, …what to add) changes the array itself.
example: po.wor planner: Enter splits a line in two; Backspace joins two lines.
remember: slice copies, splice changes (the p is for "put in").

syntax:
const queue = ["a", "b", "c"];
const first = queue.shift();   // takes "a" off the front
queue.push(first);            // puts it on the back
console.log(queue);   // b c a
explain: shift takes the first item off and gives it back. push adds to the end. Together: a queue.
example: po.wor Japanese page: questions come one by one from a shuffled queue.
remember: shift = shift everyone forward (the first one leaves). push = join the back.

explain: A fair shuffle: go from the end, swap each item with a random one before it. [a, b] = [b, a] swaps two values.
example: po.wor Japanese page: shuffles the questions.
remember: [a, b] = [b, a] = swap in one line.

explain: % is the remainder after dividing. It makes a number wrap around: past the end goes back to 0. Adding count first stops it going below 0.
example: po.wor planner: ↑ and ↓ in the suggestion list wrap around.
remember: % = remainder. Add the count first so it never goes negative.

explain: getComputedStyle gives the styles the browser really uses. parseFloat("14px") turns the text into the number 14.
example: po.wor planner: works out how wide one letter is to place the suggestion list.
remember: computed = what the browser actually uses. parseFloat reads the number at the start.

explain: getBoundingClientRect gives where an element is on screen: left, top, width, height, measured from the window's top-left corner.
example: po.wor: the P pops up beside the box; the suggestion list appears under the word.
remember: Bounding box = the rectangle around it.

syntax:
const touch = matchMedia("(hover: none)").matches;
console.log(touch ? "touch screen" : "has a mouse");
explain: matchMedia asks a CSS @media question from JavaScript. .matches is true or false.
example: po.wor: phones get the tap bubble and the bullet bar.
remember: The @media question, asked from JS.

syntax: console.log(visualViewport.height, innerHeight);
explain: On phones the keyboard covers part of the page. visualViewport is the part you can still see; innerHeight is the whole window.
example: po.wor planner: keeps the bullet bar just above the phone keyboard.
remember: visual = what you can actually see right now.

explain: animate plays keyframes from JavaScript: a list of steps, then options. offset is where a step happens (0 to 1). fill: "forwards" keeps the last step.
example: po.wor: the P that gets tossed into the box.
remember: Like @keyframes, but in JS. offset 0.2 = 20%. forwards = stay at the end.

syntax:
const DAYS = ["sunday", "monday", "tuesday", "wednesday", "thursday", "friday", "saturday"];
console.log(DAYS.findIndex((name) => name.startsWith("fri")));
explain: findIndex gives the position of the first item where your function returns true, or -1 if none.
example: po.wor: @fri finds Friday in the planner.
remember: find = the item, findIndex = where it is (-1 = nowhere).

explain: setHours(h, m, s, ms) sets the time. 0, 0, 0, 0 means midnight, so you can compare days without the time getting in the way.
example: po.wor: the planner's "today" for @day moves.
remember: Four zeros = the start of the day.

explain: setTimeout returns a number; clearTimeout(that number) cancels it. Clear the old timer before starting a new one, so only the last one runs.
example: po.wor: the "moved to Fri" note in the planner.
remember: Keep the ticket (timer), tear it up (clearTimeout).

explain: concat makes a new array: the first one followed by the second. The old arrays stay the same.
example: po.wor: a moved task goes to the end of that day.
remember: concat = chain together (a new array, nothing changed).

syntax:
const line = "    buy milk";
console.log(line.match(/^ */)[0].length);
explain: /^ */ means "spaces at the start" (zero or more). match gives an array; [0] is the matched text; .length counts the spaces.
example: po.wor: how far in a planner sub-task is.
remember: ^ = start, " *" = any number of spaces.

explain: (?: … )? is an optional group: the year part may be there or not. \d{4} is 4 digits, \d{1,2} is 1 or 2. ( ) captures each number. If the year is missing, m[1] is undefined.
example: po.wor: @11-30 and @2026-11-30 in the planner.
remember: ? after a group = "maybe". {1,2} = one or two of them.

explain: + 7 keeps it positive, % 7 wraps around the week, and || 7 turns 0 ("today") into 7 ("next week").
example: po.wor: @fri moves a task to the next Friday.
remember: Add a week, wrap the week, never zero.

syntax:
const date = new Date(2026, 2 - 1, 31);
console.log(date.getMonth() !== 2 - 1);   // true: no 31 February
explain: new Date rolls a bad day over into the next month (31 Feb becomes 3 March). If the month changed, the date was not real.
example: po.wor: @2-31 is ignored in the planner.
remember: Months start at 0. If the month moved, the date was fake.

explain: splice removes items and gives them back as a new array, so you can keep working on them with .map.
example: po.wor: moving a task and its sub-tasks to another day.
remember: splice cuts out and hands you the piece.

explain: while repeats as long as the test is true. pop removes the last item. Together: drop empty lines from the end.
example: po.wor: no gap before a moved task.
remember: while = if, again and again.

explain: el.style sets CSS from JavaScript. CSS names with a dash become camelCase (margin-left → marginLeft). The value is a string with its unit; ch is the width of one character.
example: po.wor: sub-tasks are pushed in by their spaces.
remember: Dash in CSS = capital in JS.

explain: Recursion: a function that calls itself with a smaller problem, and a stop case so it ends.
example: po.wor: show() calls itself for an indented line.
remember: Always a stop case first, then a smaller step.
builtFrom: function + if + a call to itself

explain: Keep the data in one array of objects, and let a loop build the page from it. To add a project, add one line to the list; the code doesn't change.
example: po.wor: js/footer.js builds the footer icons from PROJECTS.
remember: Data in a list, code in a loop. Add a line, not code.
builtFrom: array of objects + for...of + DOM methods

explain: location.pathname is the page's path. split("/") cuts it into parts and pop() takes the last one, the file name. On the home page the last part is "", so || gives "index.html".
example: po.wor: the footer finds which page you are on.
remember: Cut at the slashes, take the last piece, fall back with ||.

explain: + joins strings, so a long string can be split over several lines. Single quotes on the outside let the HTML use double quotes inside.
example: po.wor: the box icon's SVG in js/footer.js.
remember: End a line with +, carry on below.

explain: Event bubbling: a click on an inner element also reaches every element around it. event.stopPropagation() stops it there, so the outer click doesn't run too.
example: po.wor: clicking a bullet in the week view ticks it without opening the day.
remember: Events bubble up like air in water; stopPropagation pops the bubble.
builtFrom: two listeners + a method call on the event object

explain: Inside forEach, return only ends this one item's function, so it skips to the next item, like continue in a for loop.
example: po.wor: the week view shows only tasks and events.
remember: return in forEach = skip this one.
builtFrom: array . forEach ( arrow function with if + return )
